verdicts.why: Names the act of making or bringing forth without any stance on the maker or the thing made.
Plain statement that one party travels with another; no attitude toward either.
States co-occurrence (a yawn accompanying a remark) with no judgement of what co-occurs.
Describes being someone's companion neutrally; the speaker's feeling about the companionship is not in the word.
Names a diverting pastime; where Austen wants dismissal she has to add 'trifling', which shows the noun alone does not supply it.
A plain emotion noun for delight at being entertained; that Mr Bennet's amusement is at his wife's expense comes from context, not the word.
Neutral label for content held true; it takes no side on whether the belief is warranted.
Same neutral noun in a weaker-confidence sense; nothing about the speaker's regard for the idea.
A bare placing verb (stress laid on forms, money laid down); no evaluation of what is placed.
Imposing blame or a charge is unpleasant, but 'lay' itself is the plain verb for it; the judgement in the sentences sits in 'profligacy' and 'folly', not in 'lay'.
Physical placement, entirely descriptive.
Names a warm feeling, but the warmth is the referent; unlike 'pity' it carries no shading about the one who feels it or the one it is aimed at.
A thing that provokes surprise; the evaluation is wholly contained in the gloss ('it is a wonder that' is not admiring), and Austen's ironic use is context.
Plain emotion noun for surprise; no stance on what surprised.
Curiosity named neutrally; nothing about the speaker's attitude toward the object of curiosity.
Reports that resentment was caused without taking sides on whether the offence was deserved (Miss Lucas excuses the pride that offends).
Plain verb for hurting feelings; the fault could lie with either party and the word does not say.
Describes an effect (disgust) on the receiver; the word itself does not condemn the cause.
Abstract faculty of choice, named neutrally; the packet's sentences are all the modal verb, but the sense as glossed carries no attitude.
A legal document; purely referential.
Fixed intent, named without approval or disapproval; 'strong will' and 'stubborn will' both need the adjective to tilt it.
Forming an emotional tie, stated plainly; any excess ('excessively attached') is supplied by the adverb.
Causing one thing to be fixed to another; descriptive.
Being joined or belonging to (happiness attached to a situation, blame attaching to conduct); no judgement in the verb.
Names a fearful feeling in plain words; a bad referent, not a loaded word, and it takes no side on whether the fear is reasonable.
